Ruflo MCP Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Run Commands and Poison AI Memory

The Hacker News
2026-07-29 9 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a maximum-severity security flaw in Ruflo, an open-source agent meta-harness for Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-59726 (CVSS score: 10.0), impacts all versions of the project before version 3.16.3. It has been codenamed RufRoot by Noma Security's

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Non-loopback inbound to Ruflo MCP bridge (3001) or MongoDB (27017) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated POST /mcp tools/call to Ruflo MCP bridge (CVE-2026-59726 RufRoot) · [LLM] Ruflo MCP bridge (node) spawns a shell — terminal_execute RCE · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Backdoor payload written to /app by shell or downloader in Ruflo container
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Unauthenticated POST /mcp tools/call to Ruflo MCP bridge (CVE-2026-59726 RufRoot) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RufRoot exploit request: an unauthenticated HTTP POST to the Ruflo MCP bridge's /mcp (or /mcp/:group) endpoint on port 3001, invoking tools/call without a Bearer token. Pre-3.16.3 this returns a shell inside the bridge container. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact vulnerable endpoint, port, and missing-Authorization pattern rather than a generic web-exploit shape. Rationale: Anchored on the exact article strings: POST /mcp endpoint, port 3001, and the missing Authorization/Bearer header (patch 3.16.3 added MCP_AUTH_TOKEN bearer middleware). Defender AH has no inbound-HTTP-request table so defender_kql is intentionally blank; endpoint-side follow-through is covered by UC2/UC4. Cross-checked against: • https://noma.security/blog/rufroot-the-mcp-bridge-vulnerability-that-turns-agents-into-rogue-admins-cve-2026-59726/ • https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo/releases/tag/v3.16.3 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/critical-ruflo-mcp-bridge-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal MCP client POSTing to /mcp with a valid Bearer token (excluded by the empty-Authorization filter)
  • Vulnerability scanners / ASM tools probing /mcp on port 3001
  • Internal health-check or CI pipeline hitting the bridge endpoint
  • Load balancer / reverse proxy re-issuing requests that strip the Authorization header
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SrcIpAddr and confirm it is external / non-loopback; check the response status — a 200 to an unauthenticated POST /mcp indicates a vulnerable (pre-3.16.3) instance and likely successful exploitation. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/firewall and immediately close inbound access to ports 3001 and 27017; confirm the Ruflo image is >= 3.16.3 with MCP bound to loopback. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (shell spawned by the node bridge) and UC3 (/app writes) on the same host, and treat all LLM provider API keys in the container env as compromised — rotate them.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/mcp"
| where DstPortNumber == 3001 or Url has ":3001"
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no Bearer token = unauthenticated (patch 3.16.3 requires MCP_AUTH_TOKEN)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, EventProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Ruflo MCP bridge (node) spawns a shell — terminal_execute RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation shell: the Ruflo MCP bridge Node/Express process spawning /bin/sh (or bash/dash) as a child, which is how the terminal_execute tool obtains a shell inside the bridge container. Article-specific via the node parent whose command line references ruflo/claude-flow/mcp/agentdb/app spawning a shell child. Rationale: The bridge is confirmed (Noma, GitHub release) to be an Express.js/Node server; terminal_execute obtains a shell in the bridge container, so node→sh is the article-specific execution pivot. Datadog/Falcon add the PoC recon string 'id && hostname' plus reverse-shell markers since auditd/FDR lack parent-cmdline context. Cross-checked against: • https://noma.security/blog/rufroot-the-mcp-bridge-vulnerability-that-turns-agents-into-rogue-admins-cve-2026-59726/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/critical-ruflo-mcp-bridge-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node/npm lifecycle scripts (postinstall, prestart) shelling out during container startup
  • A Ruflo admin using an authenticated terminal_execute feature legitimately after enabling MCP_ENABLE_TERMINAL
  • node-gyp / native module builds invoking sh at runtime
  • Container entrypoint wrapper scripts that re-exec via sh
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("npm run","node-gyp","prestart","postinstall") and ParentCmd has_any ("npm","install","build"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child shell's ProcessCommandLine — recon (id, hostname, whoami), downloaders (curl/wget), or reverse-shell (/dev/tcp, nc -e) confirm hands-on-keyboard; correlate the parent node PID with an inbound POST /mcp (UC1) in the preceding seconds. 2) Contain: isolate the container/host, kill the bridge process, and block egress; snapshot the container for forensics before rebuild. 3) Hunt: check /app for dropped payloads (UC3), enumerate container env for exposed LLM API keys, and review AgentDB/MongoDB for injected agentdb_pattern-store entries (UC5). Rotate all provider keys.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","npm","npx","tsx","ts-node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ruflo","claude-flow","mcp","agentdb","/app")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs","npm","npx","tsx")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ruflo","claude-flow","mcp","agentdb","/app")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoor payload written to /app by shell or downloader in Ruflo container AIInstallation High
Hunts persistence: a shell, downloader, or scripting interpreter (not node) writing files into the /app directory of the Ruflo container — the exact persistence action the advisory calls out ('persistent backdoor deployment by writing a malicious payload to the /app directory'). Runtime writes to /app by sh/curl/wget are anomalous for a built image. Rationale: Directly anchored on the advisory's '/app directory' backdoor persistence. The high-fidelity twist is the writing process: a purpose-built Node image should not have sh/curl/wget writing into /app at runtime. Datadog auditd schema lacks file-path fields so datadog is intentionally blank. Cross-checked against: • https://noma.security/blog/rufroot-the-mcp-bridge-vulnerability-that-turns-agents-into-rogue-admins-cve-2026-59726/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Entrypoint or deploy scripts writing runtime config/templates into /app at container start
  • Application self-update or cache writes into /app by node (excluded by process filter, but wrapper shells may trigger)
  • An admin manually patching files in a running container via docker exec sh
  • Log-rotation or tee-based logging writing under /app
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("entrypoint","docker-entrypoint","start.sh") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("containerd-shim","runc","dockerd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the written file (name, hash, TargetFilePath) — scripts (.sh/.js/.py), ELF binaries, or files with world-exec bits dropped by a shell/curl are high-confidence backdoors; correlate with the writing process's parent (node/UC2). 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the container, and rebuild from a known-clean image >= 3.16.3 (an in-place delete is insufficient — the advisory mandates image rebuild). 3) Hunt: diff /app against the official image manifest, search other hosts for the same file hash, and review MongoDB/AgentDB for tampering plus rotate all provider API keys.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath startswith "/app"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","curl","wget","tee","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/app"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/curl","/wget","/tee","/python","/perl","/nc","/ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Non-loopback inbound to Ruflo MCP bridge (3001) or MongoDB (27017) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the network exposure that makes RufRoot exploitable: inbound connections to TCP 3001 (MCP bridge) or 27017 (MongoDB) from a non-loopback source. Post-3.16.3 both bind to loopback, so any remote connection — especially to unauthenticated MongoDB 27017 — indicates an exposed/attacked instance. The advisory explicitly says close ports 3001 and 27017. Rationale: Anchored on the advisory's remediation ('close firewall ports 3001 and 27017') and the 0.0.0.0 default-bind root cause; post-patch loopback binding makes any non-loopback source to these ports a reliable exposure/attack signal, with 27017 (unauthenticated MongoDB) being especially high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://noma.security/blog/rufroot-the-mcp-bridge-vulnerability-that-turns-agents-into-rogue-admins-cve-2026-59726/ • https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo/releases/tag/v3.16.3
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal application tier or reverse proxy connecting to the MCP bridge on 3001 over an internal (RFC1918) network
  • Backup or monitoring agents connecting to MongoDB 27017 from an internal management host
  • Kubernetes/service-mesh sidecar traffic reaching the bridge from a pod IP
  • Vulnerability scanners probing 3001/27017 across the estate
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the source is external/internet or an internal known service; for 27017 treat ANY non-loopback source as critical since MongoDB shipped without auth pre-3.16.3. 2) Contain: apply firewall/security-group rules to restrict 3001 and 27017 to loopback/known internal IPs, and verify the deployment is on 3.16.3 (loopback bind + MongoDB auth). 3) Hunt: correlate the source IP with UC1 (POST /mcp) and UC2 (shell spawn); if MongoDB was reachable, assume conversation data and AgentDB were read/tampered and audit for injected agentdb_pattern-store entries.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionRequest")
| where LocalPort in (3001, 27017)
| where RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1","0.0.0.0")
| extend ExposureNote = iff(LocalPort == 27017, "MongoDB - should never be non-loopback", "MCP bridge")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteIPType, ExposureNote,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DstPortNumber in (3001, 27017)          // MCP bridge + MongoDB; loopback-only after patch 3.16.3
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1","::1","0.0.0.0","localhost")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkDirection, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Three Critical VMware Flaws Allow Auth Bypass, Code Execution, and VM Escape

The Hacker News
2026-07-29 7 use cases 3 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Broadcom has released security updates to address multiple security flaws impacting VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, and Fusion, three of which have been designated as critical in severity. The first of the three critical-rated flaws is CVE-2026-59309 (CVSS score: 9.8), which has been described as an authentication bypass in VMware vCenter. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exposure hunt: vCenter auth-bypass + directory-traversal RCE (CVE-2026-59309 / CVE-2026-59310) · [LLM] Exposure hunt: ESX/ESXi VM-escape + info-disclosure host flaws (CVE-2026-47876 / CVE-2026-41703 / CVE-2026-41709) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Exposure hunt: vCenter auth-bypass + directory-traversal RCE (CVE-2026-59309 / CVE-2026-59310) AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed VMware vCenter assets carrying the two CVSS-9.8 critical vCenter flaws disclosed by Broadcom, prioritising internet-facing hosts. Both are exploitable by a network-adjacent attacker (auth bypass, and directory traversal to arbitrary code execution) so unpatched, exposed vCenter is a direct pre-auth attack surface. Rationale: Keyed on the two concrete critical CVE IDs Broadcom assigned to vCenter (CVE-2026-59309 auth bypass, CVE-2026-59310 directory-traversal RCE, both CVSS 9.8); internet-facing enrichment prioritises the exact attack surface (network access to vCenter) the advisory calls out. Fixed builds per article: 9.1.0.0300 / 9.0.2.0100 / 8.0 U3k.
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • vCenter appliance already patched to 8.0 U3k / 9.1.0.0300 / 9.0.2.0100 but TVM catalog lag still lists the CVE for a scan cycle
  • Decommissioned/offline vCenter still in asset inventory
  • Nested lab vCenter that is intentionally unpatched and network-isolated
  • TVM mis-attributing the CVE to a non-vCenter VMware component on the same host
Suppression filter
| where RecommendedSecurityUpdate != "" and toupper(VulnerabilitySeverityLevel) in ("CRITICAL","HIGH")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged host is genuinely running vCenter and check its build against the article's fixed versions (9.1.0.0300 / 9.0.2.0100 / 8.0 U3k); prioritise any row where IsInternetFacing==true. 2) Contain: restrict vCenter management ports (443/9443) to the admin jump network via firewall/NSX until patched, and apply the Broadcom async/fixed build. 3) Hunt: on confirmed-exposed hosts, review vCenter reverse-proxy/vpxd logs for anomalous unauthenticated /sdk or /api session creation and directory-traversal path patterns, and audit for any new local accounts or SSO grants.

Exposure hunt: ESX/ESXi VM-escape + info-disclosure host flaws (CVE-2026-47876 / CVE-2026-41703 / CVE-2026-41709) AIExploitation High
Surfaces VMware ESX/ESXi hypervisors carrying the three ESX-side flaws Broadcom patched, led by CVE-2026-47876 — a VMXNET3 out-of-bounds write Broadcom explicitly labels a virtual-machine escape (guest local-admin executes code on the ESX host). Covers the two lower-severity ESX info-disclosure/logging bugs on the same assets. Rationale: Keyed on the three concrete ESX CVE IDs (CVE-2026-47876 CVSS 9.3 VMXNET3 OOB-write VM escape, CVE-2026-41703 OOB read info-disclosure/DoS, CVE-2026-41709 insufficient logging) with the VMXNET3 host-escape flagged; article fixed builds ESXi-9.1.0.0200-25557999 / ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025 / ESXi80U3k-25595708 anchor the patched baseline.
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ESXi host already on fixed build (ESXi80U3k-25595708 / ESXi-9.1.0.0200-25557999) but TVM catalog still lists the CVE for a scan window
  • Standalone Workstation/Fusion install where CVE-2026-41703 impact is only info-disclosure, not host RCE
  • Air-gapped lab ESXi intentionally left unpatched
  • TVM version parsing error on custom OEM ESXi image build strings
Suppression filter
| where RecommendedSecurityUpdate != ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the asset is an ESX/ESXi host and compare its build to the article's fixed builds; treat VmEscape=="yes" (CVE-2026-47876) rows as highest priority since any guest local-admin can reach the host. 2) Contain: schedule/apply the Broadcom ESXi patch; for immediate risk reduction on the VMXNET3 escape, inventory VMs using the VMXNET3 adapter and tighten who holds local admin inside those guests. 3) Hunt: review guest VMs (esp. multi-tenant/DMZ) for recent local-admin escalation, then check the ESX host for unexpected processes/logins around suspected exploitation windows given CVE-2026-41709 can suppress ESX operation logging.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Endpoint contact with F6 fraud-campaign hosting infra (212.127.73.235 / 167.86.100.68) · [LLM] DNS / web resolution of F6 counterfeit Russian-company domains · [LLM] Inbound email from F6 fraud clone domain (ruspromexport-group.ru / info@ruspromexport-group.ru) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Endpoint contact with F6 fraud-campaign hosting infra (212.127.73.235 / 167.86.100.68) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts outbound endpoint or perimeter connections to the fixed IP addresses that host the bulk of the F6 advance-payment fraud clone sites. Any internal host resolving/reaching this infrastructure indicates a user was steered to a counterfeit Russian-company site controlled by the fraudsters. Rationale: Uses the two campaign IPs named in the article body (212.127.73.235, 167.86.100.68) that F6 states host 'the vast majority' of the ~100 clone domains, plus two related IPs from the extracted IOC set. Fixed-IP contact is a clean, deployable alert pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nine-year-fraud-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1566
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • 185.220.101.16 / 185.220.101.15 fall in known Tor exit-node ranges — benign Tor/research traffic will hit these
  • Shared-hosting neighbours: a legitimate unrelated site co-located on 212.127.73.235 could generate hits
  • Security-team sandbox detonation or threat-intel enrichment deliberately visiting the fraud sites
  • VPN/proxy egress IP overlap if the org's own egress shares a /24 with the hosting provider
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP in ("185.220.101.16","185.220.101.15") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","browser.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal src host and user, and pull the RemoteUrl/RequestURL to confirm which clone domain (e.g. ruspromexport-group.ru) was reached; confirm the two Tor-range IPs weren't just background Tor. 2) Contain: block the four IPs and known clone domains at proxy/firewall/DNS sink; warn the user and their finance team not to action any invoice or bank-detail change originating from that contact. 3) Hunt: pivot on the src host for received emails from *ruspromexport-group.ru / info@ruspromexport-group.ru and any wire-transfer/vendor-bank-change requests in the same window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("212.127.73.235","167.86.100.68","185.220.101.16","185.220.101.15")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("212.127.73.235","167.86.100.68","185.220.101.16","185.220.101.15")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS / web resolution of F6 counterfeit Russian-company domains AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS queries or web connections to the specific counterfeit domains used in the F6 fraud campaign (ruspromexport-group.ru and agrocenter-eurohem.ru, including mail/www hosts). Resolution of these lookalike domains from an internal host indicates a user is interacting with a fraudster-controlled clone of a legitimate Russian supplier. Rationale: Uses the two exact counterfeit domains named in the article (ruspromexport-group.ru and the 2017-era agrocenter-eurohem.ru clone). Domain resolution is unambiguous — these hostnames have no legitimate use, so a hit is a high-fidelity indicator with negligible FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nine-year-fraud-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or brand-protection tooling actively crawling the fraud domains for takedown
  • Security researcher / SOC analyst manually browsing the clone site during triage
  • Domain sinkhole or passive-DNS collector inside the org resolving the domain
  • Email security gateway pre-fetching URLs in a delivered message for detonation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the client host/user from ClientIP and confirm whether the resolution came from a browser (interactive visit) vs a security tool. 2) Contain: DNS-sink the domains, block at proxy, and alert the user's finance/procurement contacts to freeze any pending payment tied to that 'supplier'. 3) Hunt: search EmailEvents for messages carrying these domains or info@ruspromexport-group.ru, and pivot on the resolved IPs (UC1) to catch other clone domains on the same infrastructure.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("ruspromexport-group.ru","agrocenter-eurohem.ru")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("ruspromexport-group.ru","agrocenter-eurohem.ru")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: b71d3e29-4a6c-4f52-9c8a-1d0e6b3f7c22

detection:

      - 'ruspromexport-group.ru'

  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:(*ruspromexport-group.ru* OR *agrocenter-eurohem.ru* OR *RUSPROMEXPORT-GROUP.RU* OR *AGROCENTER-EUROHEM.RU*)

| DomainName=/(ruspromexport-group|agrocenter-eurohem)\.ru$/i

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("*ruspromexport-group.ru","*agrocenter-eurohem.ru") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("*ruspromexport-group.ru","*agrocenter-eurohem.ru") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Inbound email from F6 fraud clone domain (ruspromexport-group.ru / info@ruspromexport-group.ru) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail whose sender/envelope domain matches the fraudster-controlled clone infrastructure. F6 documented that operators send commercial offers, contracts and invoices with bogus bank details from fake corporate mailboxes such as info@ruspromexport-group.ru to route advance payments to criminal accounts. Rationale: Uses the fraud mailbox/domain named in the extracted IOC set (info@ruspromexport-group.ru, ruspromexport-group.ru, mail.ruspromexport-group.ru). Sender-domain match on a dedicated fraud clone domain is high-fidelity; the AttachmentCount projection surfaces the bogus contract/invoice PDFs F6 describes. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nine-year-fraud-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate business contact who genuinely uses a similarly-named but distinct domain (verify exact spelling)
  • Internal forward/report of the phishing sample to a security mailbox re-ingested as inbound
  • Quarantine/replay of an already-blocked message generating a second EmailEvents row
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the message, sender IP (map to UC1 infra) and any attachments; confirm the bank details in the invoice/contract differ from the legitimate supplier's on record. 2) Contain: quarantine/purge all copies, block the sender domain, and immediately notify the recipient and AP/finance to halt any wire transfer tied to this correspondence. 3) Hunt: search for other recipients of the same or lookalike domains, cross-reference the DNS/IP UCs, and check for cold-call / 'senior manager' follow-up per the campaign's social-engineering pattern.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "ruspromexport-group.ru" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "ruspromexport-group.ru" or SenderFromAddress =~ "info@ruspromexport-group.ru"
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentCount, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "ruspromexport-group.ru" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "ruspromexport-group.ru" or SenderFromAddress =~ "info@ruspromexport-group.ru"
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentCount, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Researchers Show a Single Malicious Webpage Visit Can Compromise Tor Browser

The Hacker News
2026-07-29 10 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Nebula Security says a patched Firefox JIT flaw could be triggered by simply visiting a malicious webpage and was also used to compromise Tor Browser. Tracked as CVE-2026-10702, the bug provides arbitrary code execution inside the browser's renderer process. Mozilla rated it High and fixed it in the Firefox 151.0.3 update. "No settings or additional user interaction are required," Eten Zou,

Vulnerable Firefox exposed to CVE-2026-10702 JIT RCE (147 through 151.0.2) AIExploitation High
Surfaces endpoints running a Firefox build in the vulnerable range for CVE-2026-10702, the ObjectToIterator JIT type-confusion flaw Nebula Security weaponised as IonStack stage 1. Hunts exposure since a single malicious webpage visit yields renderer RCE with no user interaction; patched only in 151.0.3 (ESR 140.12 unaffected). Rationale: Uses the exact CVE (CVE-2026-10702) and its patched build (151.0.3) from the article; a direct TVM CVE match is unambiguous exposure, no version-string parsing needed. Cross-checked against Rapid7 MFSA-2026-54 and Mozilla's advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/db/vulnerabilities/mfsa2026-54-cve-2026-10702/ • https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-54/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-10702/
ATT&CKT1203 T1189
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint patched to 151.0.3 but TVM inventory not yet re-scanned (stale snapshot shows old version)
  • Firefox ESR 140.12 mis-catalogued into the vulnerable range by the scanner (article confirms ESR is NOT affected)
  • Portable/second Firefox install TVM cannot version-resolve, reported as generic 'firefox'
  • Developer/nightly channel builds carrying a version string outside the stable range
  • Kiosk or air-gapped hosts that never touch the internet (exposure present but exploit path blocked)
Suppression filter
| where not (SoftwareName has "esr" and SoftwareVersion startswith "140.12")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely <=151.0.2 (or ESR <140.12) and the host has browser internet access; discount ESR 140.12 hits. 2) Contain: push Firefox 151.0.3 (or ESR 140.12) via patch management; for high-value hosts, temporarily restrict outbound browsing until updated. 3) Hunt: on any host that browsed before patching, pivot to UC 'Firefox renderer process spawning child' to check for actual renderer RCE, and review proxy logs for the browsing that preceded any anomaly.

Outdated Tor Browser bundling vulnerable Firefox (CVE-2026-10702 exposure) AIExploitation Medium
Tor Browser bundles Firefox and is not catalogued by vulnerability scanners, so TVM misses it. This hunts running Tor Browser firefox.exe instances, parses the bundled Firefox product version, and flags builds in the 147 through 151.0.2 range vulnerable to the IonStack stage-1 JIT RCE. Directly addresses the article's headline that every Tor Browser release carrying a vulnerable Firefox is affected. Rationale: Article headline is Tor-Browser-specific and TVM cannot see Tor's bundled Firefox, so this parses ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion against the exact vulnerable range (147–151.0.2, patched 151.0.3) and scopes to the 'Tor Browser' install path. Version-range logic mirrors the article's stated affected range. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researchers-show-single-malicious.html • https://security.lookout.com/threat-intelligence/article/cve-2026-10702-firefox-for-android-jit-type-confusion-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1203 T1189
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User already updated Tor Browser but an old cached process execution still sits in the 14-day window
  • Tor Browser Alpha/nightly channel reporting a non-stable version string that mis-parses
  • Portable Tor Browser run from a USB/Downloads path not containing 'Tor Browser' folder name (missed, not FP — coverage gap)
  • Version info field blank on some builds, yielding null Major (row dropped, not FP)
  • Legitimate privacy-conscious users for whom Tor usage itself is sanctioned — exposure is real but not malicious activity
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parsed Version is truly <=151.0.2 and the Tor Browser is actively used (recent LastSeen). 2) Contain: instruct user to update Tor Browser to the release bundling Firefox 151.0.3+, or remove unsanctioned Tor installs per policy. 3) Hunt: correlate the host's Tor usage window against UC 'Firefox renderer spawning child' and any local privilege-escalation signals (GhostLock CVE-2026-43499), since browser patching does not remove the kernel LPE.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "firefox.exe"
| where FolderPath has "Tor Browser" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Tor Browser"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend Ver = ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion
| extend P = split(Ver, ".")
| extend Major = toint(P[0]), Minor = toint(P[1]), Build = toint(P[2])
| where Major >= 147 and Major <= 151          // vulnerable Firefox range per article
| where not (Major == 151 and Build >= 3)        // 151.0.3 is the patched build
| summarize LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Version=any(Ver), FolderPath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, AccountName, Major, Minor, Build
| order by LastSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "firefox.exe"
| where TargetProcessName has "Tor Browser" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "Tor Browser" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "Tor Browser"
| extend Ver = ActingProcessFileVersion
| extend P = split(Ver, ".")
| extend Major = toint(P[0]), Build = toint(P[2])
| where Major >= 147 and Major <= 151
| where not (Major == 151 and Build >= 3)
| summarize LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Version=any(Ver) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Major
| order by LastSeen desc

Firefox/Tor renderer (content) process spawning an unexpected child — sandbox escape / RCE AIExploitation Medium
Detects a Firefox content/renderer process (firefox.exe launched with -contentproc) spawning a non-Firefox child process. Renderer processes are sandboxed and normally spawn nothing; a child indicates code execution inside the renderer — the exact CVE-2026-10702 primitive (arbitrary code execution in the browser's renderer process) and the pivot toward the GhostLock kernel stage. Architecture-independent per Nebula, so relevant on desktop Windows/Linux. Rationale: Grounds on the article's core primitive ('arbitrary code execution inside the browser's renderer process') and Firefox's own multiprocess architecture: the -contentproc flag uniquely marks the sandboxed renderer, and a renderer spawning any non-Firefox child is a high-fidelity sandbox-escape/RCE signal that precedes the GhostLock kernel stage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-54/ • https://www.cyberkendra.com/2026/06/one-malicious-link-full-root-access.html
ATT&CKT1203 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Firefox invoking the OS default handler for a downloaded file or a custom URL-scheme protocol (e.g. opening a PDF/mailto) from a content process
  • WebRTC/native-messaging host or browser extension helper legitimately launched from the content process
  • Third-party AV/DLP injecting into and spawning from firefox.exe
  • Crash-handling helpers not in the exclusion list on niche builds
  • Enterprise browser-management agents shelling out from Firefox context
Suppression filter
| where ChildProcess !in~ ("AcroRd32.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe") and ChildPath !has "\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process image, path and command line — LOLBins (cmd, powershell, sh, /tmp payloads) or unsigned binaries from the renderer are near-certain true positives; a signed OS file handler is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Firefox process tree, and capture volatile memory for the renderer PID before reboot. 3) Hunt: check the host for CVE-2026-43499/GhostLock local-privilege-escalation activity (unexpected root/SYSTEM child from the same tree), review proxy logs for the malicious page visited immediately prior, and confirm Firefox/Tor build against the vulnerable-version UCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "firefox.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-contentproc"   // the sandboxed renderer/content child
| where FileName !in~ ("firefox.exe","plugin-container.exe","updater.exe","crashreporter.exe","pingsender.exe","minidump-analyzer.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, RendererCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildPath = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "firefox.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-contentproc"
| where not(TargetProcessName has_any ("firefox.exe","plugin-container.exe","updater.exe","crashreporter.exe","pingsender.exe","minidump-analyzer.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RendererCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Firefox Renderer Content Process Spawning Unexpected Child
id: 5f2a1c94-7b6e-4a2d-9e3f-1c8d0a4b7e21
description: A Firefox content/renderer process (firefox.exe with -contentproc) spawns a non-Firefox child, indicating code execution inside the sandboxed renderer consistent with CVE-2026-10702 (IonStack stage 1).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researchers-show-single-malicious.html

  - attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: process_creation

Endpoint exposed to GhostLock kernel futex LPE (CVE-2026-43499, IonStack stage 2) AIExploitation Low
Surfaces Linux hosts exposed to CVE-2026-43499 (GhostLock), the kernel futex flaw Nebula uses as IonStack's second stage to carry renderer RCE to root. The article explicitly warns that patching Firefox blocks the browser entry point but does NOT patch GhostLock, so this exposure must be tracked independently of the browser fix. Rationale: Uses the article's second CVE (CVE-2026-43499 / GhostLock) and its explicit operational caveat that the kernel flaw persists after Firefox is patched; TVM CVE match gives clean, independent LPE-exposure tracking for the privilege-escalation phase. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researchers-show-single-malicious.html • https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319914/20260708/public-exploit-turns-15-year-linux-kernel-flaw-5-second-root-attack.htm
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host kernel already patched but TVM snapshot stale, still showing the CVE
  • Backported vendor kernel (RHEL/Ubuntu) where the fix is applied but version string still matches the scanner's vulnerable pattern
  • Containers inheriting the host kernel version double-counted as separate assets
  • Embedded/appliance Linux where the futex path is not reachable in practice
  • Non-Android Linux hosts with no browser present (exposure real but full IonStack chain not applicable)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the running kernel is genuinely unpatched (uname -r vs vendor fixed build) and not a backport false match. 2) Contain: schedule/expedite kernel patching; for internet-facing or browser-heavy hosts, prioritise since GhostLock is invoked directly from the browser. 3) Hunt: on exposed hosts, review for renderer-escape activity (UC: Firefox renderer spawning child) and any unexpected transition to root/uid 0 from a user-context process, which would indicate GhostLock was actually fired.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
