Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

Critical OpenWrt DHCPv6 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code as Root

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 9 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

OpenWrt has shipped version 24.10.8 to close a critical DHCPv6 stack overflow and a wider set of remotely triggerable flaws in network services enabled by default. The critical issue, tracked as CVE-2026-53921 and rated 9.8 on CVSS 3.1 in OpenWrt's GitHub advisory, lets an unauthenticated attacker able to reach the DHCPv6 server overwrite a stack buffer in odhcpd through a crafted DHCPv6

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound DHCPv6 to odhcpd (UDP 547) from non-link-local source — CVE-2026-53921 exploit reach · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] LuCI luci-app-commands / ddns command injection with shell metacharacters — root RCE · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Inbound DHCPv6 to odhcpd (UDP 547) from non-link-local source — CVE-2026-53921 exploit reach AIDelivery Medium
Hunts remote reachability of the vulnerable odhcpd DHCPv6 service. Legitimate DHCPv6 clients source from link-local fe80::/10; a REQUEST/SOLICIT to UDP 547 arriving from a routed/global address (or one source fanning out to many router targets) indicates remote exploitation of the CVE-2026-53921 stack overflow or scanning for it. Rationale: Article pins the trigger to an unauthenticated DHCPv6 REQUEST on UDP 547 with AV:N; the link-local-source exclusion is the discriminator between normal DHCPv6 (fe80:: sources) and remote reach of odhcpd. Corroborated by the odhcpd advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/openwrt/odhcpd/security/advisories/GHSA-7fwx-hhrg-3496 • https://github.com/openwrt/odhcpd/security/advisories/GHSA-7hcw-g2jh-pqv5
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DHCPv6 relay agent (dhcp6relay) legitimately forwarding requests from a non-link-local relay address
  • Managed WAN/ISP DHCPv6 prefix-delegation clients hitting the router's server
  • Internal IPv6 network scanner / vuln-scanner probing UDP 547 during authorized assessment
  • Misconfigured DHCPv6 client on a routed VLAN sourcing from a global address
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceIP in ("<known_dhcp6relay_ips>")) // maintain relay allowlist if relays present
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/routed (not a known relay); check whether the same source hit multiple OpenWrt devices (Targets>1 = scanning). 2) Contain: block UDP 547 inbound from WAN/untrusted segments at the firewall; verify odhcpd is on 24.10.8/25.12.5. 3) Hunt: pivot to that device's Syslog for odhcpd segfaults/respawns (see crash UC) and any root shell spawned shortly after the packet.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort == 547
| where not(SourceIP startswith "fe80" or SourceIP startswith "FE80")   // legit DHCPv6 clients use link-local source addresses
| summarize Requests=count(), Targets=dcount(DestinationIP), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where Targets >= 1
| order by Requests desc
NETWORK

| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")`
| where NOT match(src,"(?i)^fe80")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - conn_count
| tstats summariesonly=false count as conn_count dc(All_Traffic.dest) as target_count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.transport=udp All_Traffic.dest_port=547 by All_Traffic.src

LuCI luci-app-commands / ddns command injection with shell metacharacters — root RCE AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to LuCI command/DDNS endpoints carrying a bare pipe or other shell metacharacters. Hacker House's findings: luci-app-commands lets a bare '|' bypass the argument allow-list (unauthenticated when a command is public='1' param='1'), and ddns_dateformat / luci-proto-openvpn keytype inject into root-run shell operations. Rationale: Article/advisory give concrete injection points: the bare pipe in luci-app-commands and ddns_dateformat/keytype reaching root shell. Matching those exact endpoint tokens plus a shell metacharacter (raw or URL-encoded) is high-fidelity for the reported command-injection paths. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-openwrt-dhcpv6-flaw-could-let.html • https://www.cybersecurity-help.cz/vulnerabilities/55591/ • https://github.com/openwrt/luci/issues/6977
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately using luci-app-commands to chain commands with a pipe (intended feature for authenticated admins)
  • DDNS date-format string that legitimately contains a semicolon or backtick-free format token
  • Automation/Ansible pushing UCI config that includes a keytype value with special chars
  • WAF/security scanner replaying command-injection test payloads against the router
Suppression filter
// keep only requests lacking a valid session where the app should require one:
| where SyslogMessage !has "authenticated" or SyslogMessage has "public"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source IP and whether the request had a valid session cookie/CSRF token; an unauthenticated hit on a public='1' param='1' command is a confirmed pre-auth RCE. 2) Contain: block the source, disable the exposed public parameterised command / luci-app-commands, and rotate router credentials. 3) Hunt: review Syslog for the resulting root command output, new cron/init.d persistence, added SSH keys, and outbound connections from the device following the request.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("luci-app-commands","/cgi-bin/luci/command","admin/system/commands","ddns_dateformat","luci-proto-openvpn","keytype")
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(%7c|\||%3b|;|%60|`|\$\(|%24%28)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.http_method) as method from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*luci/command/*" OR Web.url="*admin/system/commands*" OR Web.url="*ddns_dateformat=*" OR Web.url="*keytype=*") by Web.src Web.dest

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

cgi-io path traversal reading root files — CVE-2026-62947 AIActions on Objectives High
Detects requests to the OpenWrt cgi-io download endpoint containing directory-traversal sequences aimed at root-readable files (e.g. /etc/shadow). CVE-2026-62947 lets a session holding cgi-io download permission with a wildcard file-read grant traverse out and disclose arbitrary root-readable files. Rationale: CVE-2026-62947 is a cgi-io path-traversal file read of root-readable files; matching the cgi-io endpoint together with ../ or %2e%2e or an /etc/ target is a precise signature for the disclosed exploitation attempt. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-openwrt-dhcpv6-flaw-could-let.html • https://vulners.com/search/types/openwrt
ATT&CKT1190 T1003.008
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate LuCI backup/download of a config file whose path happens to contain '/etc/config'
  • Admin using cgi-io to download a firmware/log file with a relative path in the URL
  • Security scanner testing traversal payloads against the router
  • URL-decoding artifact where a benign filename contains '..' as literal characters
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(\.\./|%2e%2e)"  // require an actual traversal token, not just an /etc/config download
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the traversal target (../../etc/shadow vs a benign /etc/config download) and whether the session had legitimate cgi-io download + wildcard grant. 2) Contain: revoke the over-broad wildcard file-read ACL, invalidate the session, and rotate any credentials in files that may have been disclosed. 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct file path this source requested via cgi-io, and check whether disclosed secrets (shadow hashes, keys) were subsequently used to authenticate.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "cgi-io"
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(\.\./|%2e%2e|/etc/(shadow|passwd|config)|%2fetc%2f)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.http_method) as method from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*cgi-io*" by Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| where match(url,"(?i)(\.\./|%2e%2e|/etc/(shadow|passwd|config)|%2fetc%2f)")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NightLedger recon: access to C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log by non-system process
NightLedger DLL side-load: AppVShNotify.exe loading SspiCli.dll from non-System32 AIInstallation High
Hunts Nimbus Manticore's NightLedger backdoor, which is delivered as a malicious SspiCli.dll DLL search-order-hijacked into the legitimate signed Microsoft App-V binary AppVShNotify.exe. Legitimate SspiCli.dll only ever loads from System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS, so a load from any user-writable directory by AppVShNotify.exe is the side-load itself. Rationale: Uses the exact side-load pair confirmed by TechNadu's write-up of the same Kaspersky research (NightLedger = malicious SspiCli.dll search-order-hijacked into legitimate AppVShNotify.exe). Legit SspiCli.dll is a protected System32 DLL, so a load from a user-writable path is deterministic evidence of the hijack. Cross-checked against: • https://www.technadu.com/mirage-kittens-new-malware-toolkit-targets-aerospace-and-defense-across-middle-east-and-africa/632036/ • https://securelist.com/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1574.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate App-V (Application Virtualization) streaming that stages AppVShNotify.exe in a package cache under ProgramData
  • Software packaging/repackaging tools that copy AppVShNotify.exe into a build or staging directory
  • Portable-app frameworks bundling App-V components in a non-standard folder
  • Security testing / red-team side-load simulation of SspiCli.dll
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData\App-V\") and not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Application Virtualization\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full path AppVShNotify.exe launched from and the SspiCli.dll hash; a legitimate SspiCli.dll is Microsoft-signed and lives only in System32 — an unsigned copy in a user dir confirms NightLedger. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the DLL and the containing folder for analysis, and block the SHA256. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for outbound HTTPS beacons from AppVShNotify.exe, access to C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log, and co-resident unbcl.dll/libwinpthread-1.dll (BridgeHead) drops.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AppVShNotify.exe"
| where FileName =~ "SspiCli.dll"
| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedFrom = FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\AppVShNotify.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Windows\") and not(NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Program Files")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BridgeHead SOCKS5 relay drop: unbcl.dll + libwinpthread-1.dll co-located outside System32 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the BridgeHead WebSocket/SOCKS5 tunneler that turns victims into covert relays. BridgeHead ships as a malicious unbcl.dll paired with the MinGW runtime libwinpthread-1.dll; the legitimate unbcl.dll is a Windows System32 DLL that never sits in a user directory, and libwinpthread-1.dll is a MinGW artifact rarely present on corporate endpoints — their co-drop in one non-Windows folder is high-fidelity. Rationale: TechNadu's coverage of the Kaspersky research confirms BridgeHead is deployed as unbcl.dll AND libwinpthread-1.dll and acts as a SOCKS5 relay. The co-drop of a spoofed System32 DLL with a MinGW pthreads runtime in a single user-writable folder is a near-unique fingerprint of the toolkit's build. Cross-checked against: • https://www.technadu.com/mirage-kittens-new-malware-toolkit-targets-aerospace-and-defense-across-middle-east-and-africa/632036/ • https://securelist.com/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1572 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations with MinGW/MSYS2 toolchains legitimately shipping libwinpthread-1.dll next to compiled binaries
  • Open-source apps bundled with MinGW runtimes (some ffmpeg/GnuPG builds) that also carry a vendored unbcl-named DLL
  • Software installers extracting DLLs to %TEMP% before moving them to Program Files
  • Portable printing/imaging utilities that ship a private copy of unbcl.dll
Suppression filter
| where not(Droppers has_any ("msys2.exe","mingw32-make.exe","cargo.exe","gcc.exe")) and not(DropDir has_any (@"\msys64\", @"\MinGW\", @"\.rustup\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm both DLLs landed in the same non-Windows folder and check unbcl.dll's signature — the legit one is Microsoft-signed in System32; an unsigned copy alongside libwinpthread-1.dll is BridgeHead. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture outbound WebSocket/HTTPS sessions — BridgeHead relays operator TCP traffic, so this host may be proxying attacker tooling into your network. 3) Hunt: review firewall/proxy for long-lived TLS WebSocket egress from the loader process and pivot to other internal hosts whose traffic egressed via this relay.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ ("unbcl.dll","libwinpthread-1.dll")
| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\")
| extend DropDir = tostring(parse_path(FolderPath).DirectoryPath)
| summarize Dlls = make_set(FileName), Droppers = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, DropDir
| where set_has_element(Dlls, "unbcl.dll") and set_has_element(Dlls, "libwinpthread-1.dll")
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("unbcl.dll","libwinpthread-1.dll")
| where not(TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\Windows\")
| summarize Dlls = make_set(TargetFileName), Actors = make_set(ActingProcessName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath
| where set_has_element(Dlls, "unbcl.dll") and set_has_element(Dlls, "libwinpthread-1.dll")
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: BridgeHead Tunneler DLL Drop (unbcl.dll / libwinpthread-1.dll) Outside System32

NightLedger recon: access to C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log by non-system process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts NightLedger's distinctive reconnaissance command that collects C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log (the domain-join troubleshooting log) alongside a process listing. This diagnostic file is almost never read by user-context software, so access or exfil-staging by a non-machine account is a strong article-specific signal. Rationale: The article explicitly lists "Collect C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log together with process-list output" as a NightLedger command — a highly unusual target file. CrowdStrike FileOpenInfo captures the read directly; Defender/Sentinel/Sysmon catch staged copies of the file created outside its canonical debug directory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.technadu.com/mirage-kittens-new-malware-toolkit-targets-aerospace-and-defense-across-middle-east-and-africa/632036/
ATT&CKT1005 T1057
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk/sysadmin manually copying NetSetup.log while troubleshooting a failed domain join
  • Endpoint management agents (SCCM/Intune) collecting diagnostic logs into a bundle
  • Backup software imaging C:\Windows\debug
  • Security IR tools sweeping diagnostic logs during an investigation
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","CompatTelRunner.exe")) and not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\CCM\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that opened/copied NetSetup.log — if it is AppVShNotify.exe or an unsigned binary in a user path, treat as NightLedger recon. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the process and any staged copy of the log for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate with the NightLedger side-load detection (SspiCli.dll into AppVShNotify.exe), screenshot-capture activity, and outbound HTTPS POST beacons from the same process indicating exfil of the collected recon bundle.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "NetSetup.log"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe","TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","MsMpEng.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "NetSetup.log"
| where not(ActingProcessName in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe","TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","MsMpEng.exe"))
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\NetSetup.log OR *\\netsetup.log) -@Image:(C:\\Windows\\System32\\svchost.exe OR *\\services.exe OR *\\TiWorker.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/\\debug\\NetSetup\.log$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(services|svchost|TiWorker|TrustedInstaller|MsMpEng)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="NetSetup.log" NOT Filesystem.file_path="C:\\Windows\\debug\\NetSetup.log" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="NetSetup.log" NOT Filesystem.file_path="C:\\Windows\\debug\\NetSetup.log" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
HOLLOWGRAPH M365 calendar dead-drop: events dated 2050-05-13 via Graph API AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Cavern Manticore HOLLOWGRAPH implant referenced in this article, which abuses the Microsoft Graph API to turn a compromised M365 mailbox calendar into a two-way C2 channel. Both tasking and exfil events are pinned to the far-future date 2050-05-13 with encrypted payloads attached as files, making that literal date string a durable hunting IOC in cloud-app audit telemetry. Rationale: Group-IB and BleepingComputer confirm HOLLOWGRAPH pulls tasking from and exfiltrates to a calendar event fixed at 2050-05-13. Matching that literal date inside CloudAppEvents RawEventData is a precise, low-FP hunt. Sentinel is left empty because OfficeActivity does not expose the calendar-event body/date needed to match 2050-05-13 — this hunt requires Defender XDR CloudAppEvents (or the raw M365 unified audit log, covered by the Splunk query). Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-hollowgraph-malware-uses-microsoft-graph-for-stealthy-c2-comms/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowgraph-malware-hides-c2-and-stolen.html
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1567.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or app legitimately creating a placeholder / 'never expire' calendar event dated in 2050
  • Test automation or calendar-sync tools generating far-future sentinel events
  • Reminder apps that use year-2050 as a 'no end date' marker
  • Data-retention or legal-hold tooling stamping far-future dates
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the RawEventData for the flagged event — confirm it is a calendar item with a file attachment and originates from a Graph API application/non-interactive session rather than the mailbox owner's client. 2) Contain: revoke the compromised mailbox's tokens, review and remove suspicious OAuth app grants (Calendars.ReadWrite / Mail scopes), and force credential reset. 3) Hunt: enumerate other mailboxes in the tenant holding 2050-dated calendar events, review Graph API sign-ins for the same app ID/IPs, and pull the attached files for RSA-encrypted payload analysis.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where tostring(RawEventData) has "2050-05-13"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Application, ActionType, ObjectName, ObjectType, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where tostring(RawEventData) has "2050-05-13"
| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Application, ActionType, ObjectName, ObjectType, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=Exchange (Operation="Create" OR Operation="Update" OR Operation="CalendarItemCreated" OR Operation="CalendarItemModified") "2050-05-13"
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Operation) as operations values(ClientIP) as client_ips by user, Subject
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — IR Trends Q2 2026: Phishing and weaponized remote management tools drive attack
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployed for headless remote control (Warlock/Storm-2603) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Trojanized MeshAgent covert backdoor: SYSTEM service beaconing over WSS (Sinobi) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Trojanized MeshAgent covert backdoor: SYSTEM service beaconing over WSS (Sinobi) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Sinobi ransomware C2 technique of weaponizing an open-source MeshCentral MeshAgent binary into a SYSTEM-level auto-start service that beacons over encrypted WebSocket (WSS/443) to an attacker server, blending with legit RMM traffic. Surfaces MeshAgent processes launched by services.exe running as SYSTEM with public outbound connections that are not part of a sanctioned MeshCentral deployment. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit, novel Sinobi tradecraft: MeshAgent weaponized as a SYSTEM auto-start service beaconing over WSS/443. Pinning the parent to services.exe + SYSTEM integrity + public egress separates a covert backdoor from an analyst manually running the tool. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1219 T1071.001 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned MeshCentral/MeshAgent RMM deployment where the org legitimately runs the agent as a SYSTEM service
  • MSP-managed endpoints beaconing to the MSP's MeshCentral server over 443
  • Security-team red-team infrastructure using MeshCentral
  • IT re-imaging workflow that reinstalls the RMM agent fleet-wide
  • MeshAgent update process reconnecting to a new public relay
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessSHA256 !in ("<approved_meshagent_sha256>") and RemoteIP !in ("<sanctioned_meshcentral_ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the destination IP/host maps to a sanctioned MeshCentral server; check the MeshAgent SHA256 against your known-good RMM binary and inspect the auto-start service name/ImagePath for anomalies. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, isolate the host, disable/delete the rogue service, and block the C2 IP at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the C2 IP across all hosts, look for subsequent RDP/WinRM lateral movement, ntds.dit access, rclone.exe staging, and GPO logon-script changes indicating imminent .SINOBI encryption.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("meshagent.exe","meshagent64.exe","meshagent-signed.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel in ("System","High") or InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "system"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), RemoteUrls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10), Conns=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("meshagent.exe","meshagent64.exe","meshagent-signed.exe") or TargetProcessName has_any ("meshagent.exe","meshagent64.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has "services.exe" or ActingProcessIntegrityLevel in ("System","High")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised M365 mailbox fan-out of QR-code PDF phishing (UAT-11764) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts UAT-11764's self-propagating QR phishing: a compromised internal M365 account blasts auto-generated PDF attachments (carrying QR codes to M365 credential-harvest pages) to large numbers of internal/external contacts harvested from the mailbox. Detects the propagation burst rather than the inbound lure, since the QR URL is embedded in a PDF image and evades URL scanning. Rationale: Targets the article's stated propagation mechanism (compromised M365 account + auto-generated victim-tailored PDF + internal contact-list expansion). Detecting the outbound/intra-org PDF fan-out from a single sender is higher-fidelity than scanning inbound mail because the QR lure hides inside a PDF image. Sentinel/Sigma/Datadog/Falcon/CWL left empty: mail-flow attachment telemetry is not present in those schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003

  • Marketing/newsletter sender blasting PDF flyers to distribution lists
  • Legal e-signature workflow sending PDF contracts to many recipients
  • Automated report mailbox (statements, receipts) with hourly PDF bursts
  • Mailing-list relay account forwarding PDF attachments org-wide
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromAddress !in~ ("payroll@yourorg.com","invoices@yourorg.com","newsletter@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the sender's recent sign-in (SigninLogs) for impossible-travel/AiTM indicators and inspect one sample PDF for an embedded QR pointing to a non-corporate M365 look-alike domain. 2) Contain: if compromised, revoke sessions, force password reset, remove any attacker inbox rules, and quarantine/purge the outbound PDF wave via ZAP. 3) Hunt: enumerate all recipients (internal + external) for clicks and secondary compromise, and check SharePoint for attacker-staged malicious documents from this account.

ARToken/EvilTokens device-code phishing: contact with pamconj C2 and Cloudflare Workers lures AIDelivery High
Detects endpoints resolving or connecting to confirmed ARToken PhaaS infrastructure — dashboard-bl.pamconj.com / spx.pamconj.com C2 and the Cloudflare Workers device-code lure hosts (clear90489058903-document.workers.dev and the {uuid}-docviewer/onedrive/adobe2.workers.dev pattern) — used to run OAuth device-authorization-flow phishing that bypasses MFA and steals Primary Refresh Tokens. Rationale: Uses concrete, second-source-confirmed IOCs: the Talos ARToken write-up independently lists dashboard-bl.pamconj.com (panel), spx.pamconj.com (C2) and the workers.dev device-code lure hosts. Fixed-string domain/DNS matches are near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/analyst detonating the ARToken lure in a sandboxed browser on a monitored host
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving IOC domains for validation
  • URL sandbox/detonation appliance (Defender/Proofpoint) fetching the workers.dev host
  • Legitimate unrelated {uuid}-docviewer.workers.dev app coincidentally matching the loose regex (verify against the exact UUID pattern)
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the query as it blocks it
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and DeviceName !in ("<sandbox_host>","<ti_enrichment_host>")

1) Triage: identify the user/host and whether the connection reached a device-code page; immediately review that user's SigninLogs for a successful 'Microsoft Authentication Broker' device-code sign-in and any new device registration. 2) Contain: revoke refresh tokens/PRTs and sessions, block the domains at DNS/proxy, and enforce a Conditional Access re-auth. 3) Hunt: check for follow-on inbox-rule creation, mailbox delegate/OAuth grant changes, and SharePoint/OneDrive exfiltration API activity from the account.

Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployed for headless remote control (Warlock/Storm-2603) AIInstallation Medium
Detects installation/execution of the Zoho Assist Unattended Agent — the RMM tool Warlock (Storm-2603) operators deployed for persistent, sessionless administrative remote control. Focuses on the unattended-agent service binaries and installer being run, particularly when dropped from user-writable/temp paths or spawned by scripting hosts rather than a sanctioned software-deployment channel. Rationale: Anchors on the article's specific finding that Warlock deployed the Zoho Assist Unattended Agent for sessionless control; the Unattended-Agent binaries + silent/unattended install flags + user-writable drop path separate attacker abuse from a helpdesk-sanctioned Zoho rollout. Storm-2603 attribution corroborated by ReliaQuest/Microsoft. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-storm-2603-exploits-CVE-2026-23760-to-stage-warlock-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk legitimately deploying Zoho Assist Unattended Agent for remote support
  • MSP onboarding endpoints with their sanctioned Zoho Assist tenant
  • Software-deployment tool (SCCM/Intune) pushing a signed Zoho MSI from a system path
  • Existing Zoho Assist agent auto-updating itself
  • User self-installing Zoho Assist for a legitimate support session
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "CCM\\Cache"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Zoho Assist is an approved RMM tool and whether this install matches a change ticket; inspect the installing user, source path, and the Zoho account/tenant the agent connects to. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, uninstall the agent, remove its service, and block Zoho Assist gateway domains at egress for the affected segment. 3) Hunt: search for the same agent across other hosts, review for concurrent MeshAgent/other RMM tooling, and check for pre-ransomware behaviors (credential dumping, GPO changes, shadow-copy deletion).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has_any ("ZohoAssist.exe","ZA_Access.exe","ZohoURSService.exe","ZMAgent.exe","Zohours.exe","ZohoAssistMsiInstaller.exe")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "Zoho" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Unattended","-install","--install","-silent","/S"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ZohoAssist.exe","ZA_Access.exe","ZohoURSService.exe","ZMAgent.exe","Zohours.exe","ZohoAssistMsiInstaller.exe")
   or (CommandLine has "Zoho" and CommandLine has_any ("Unattended","-install","--install","-silent","/S"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Domain-wide Sinobi ransomware encryption: mass .SINOBI file writes AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on the terminal Sinobi impact stage — rapid creation/rename of files bearing the .SINOBI extension across a host, consistent with domain-wide encryption pushed via a malicious GPO logon script. High-fidelity single-IOC (the .SINOBI extension) with a mass-count guard to fire only on real encryption bursts. Rationale: The .SINOBI extension is a concrete, article-stated IOC unique to this ransomware family; the 10-minute >50-file guard makes it an alerting-grade encryption-burst signal rather than a per-event dashboard. Ties to the GPO-logon-script domain-wide deployment described by Talos. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1486 T1484.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A file/backup archive that coincidentally uses a .SINOBI-named custom extension (extremely rare)
  • Malware-analysis/detonation lab intentionally running a Sinobi sample on a monitored VM
  • Restoration test re-writing previously-encrypted .SINOBI artifacts from backup
  • Security team replaying an incident sample for detection tuning
  • Forensic tooling copying encrypted evidence files, inflating the count on a collector host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("<malware_lab_host>","<forensic_collector>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the encrypting process (InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256) and the initiating account; determine whether it launched from a GPO logon-script context (parent explorer.exe/cmd.exe at logon) or a service account. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host, kill the process, disable the implicated GPO/logon script in SYSVOL, and disable the abused service account. 3) Hunt: scope the .SINOBI extension across the whole estate to gauge blast radius, review recent GPO modifications, and hunt for the MeshAgent C2, ntds.dit access, and rclone exfiltration that preceded encryption.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".SINOBI"
| summarize FileCount=count(), Folders=dcount(FolderPath), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Proc=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName,5), ProcHash=make_set(InitiatingProcessSHA256,5) by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where FileCount > 50   // 50+ .SINOBI writes in 10m = active encryption burst
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".SINOBI" or TargetFileExtension =~ "SINOBI"
| summarize FileCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Proc=make_set(ActingProcessName,5) by DvcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileCount > 50
| order by FirstSeen desc

rclone cloud-exfiltration staging prior to Sinobi encryption AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the rclone.exe data-staging/exfiltration observed in the Sinobi engagement. Matches rclone by name and by embedded original-filename metadata (catching renamed copies) executing with transfer subcommands and cloud remotes, the classic double-extortion staging step before .SINOBI encryption. Rationale: Article explicitly states data-exfiltration staging via rclone.exe in the Sinobi engagement. Matching on OriginalFileName metadata catches the common attacker practice of renaming rclone, and the transfer-subcommand + cloud-remote combo keeps FPs low. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps/backup engineer legitimately using rclone to sync data to sanctioned S3/B2 buckets
  • Sanctioned nightly cloud-backup job invoking rclone via scheduled task
  • Media/research team bulk-transferring datasets to cloud storage with rclone
  • Migration project temporarily using rclone to move file shares to OneDrive/SharePoint
  • Home-directory backup script using rclone to a corporate cloud remote
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "Backup" and AccountName !in~ ("svc-backup","svc-rclone")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the rclone config/remote target in the command line and confirm whether the destination is a sanctioned corporate cloud account or an attacker-controlled remote; review the executing account and data volume. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, kill the process, block the destination endpoint, isolate the host, and preserve the rclone.conf for scope of staged data. 3) Hunt: identify which shares/mailboxes were read, correlate with prior MeshAgent C2 and lateral RDP/WinRM, and watch for imminent .SINOBI encryption across the domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "rclone.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "rclone.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "rclone"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("copy","copyto","sync","move","--config","--transfers","--multi-thread","mega:","b2:","s3:","gdrive:","dropbox:",":pass")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "rclone.exe" or (CommandLine has_any ("copyto","--config","--transfers","--multi-thread") and CommandLine has_any ("mega:","b2:","s3:","gdrive:","dropbox:"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Post-compromise malicious inbox rule for defense evasion (UAT-11764 / ARToken BEC) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects attacker-created Exchange Online inbox rules that hide or auto-delete mail after M365 account takeover — the post-compromise defense-evasion step both UAT-11764 and ARToken affiliates use to suppress phishing replies and security notifications while propagating internally and running BEC. Rationale: Article states UAT-11764 creates inbox rules for defense evasion post-compromise and ARToken exposes inbox-rule manipulation endpoints. Filtering on hide/delete/forward rule parameters isolates the evasion intent from benign organizing rules. SPL/Sigma/Falcon/CWL empty: this is M365 audit telemetry not present in those sources. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User creating a legitimate rule to move newsletters to Deleted Items or a subfolder
  • Executive assistant setting up a forward/redirect rule for delegated mailbox management
  • User auto-marking low-priority list mail as read
  • Migration/cleanup rule bulk-moving old mail to an archive folder
  • Helpdesk configuring an approved auto-forward for a shared mailbox
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientIP in ("<corp_egress_range>") and Parameters has "MoveToFolder" and Parameters !has_any ("DeleteMessage","ForwardTo","RedirectTo"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the rule-creation ClientIP with the user's normal sign-in geo/ASN (SigninLogs) and check for a preceding device-code or AiTM sign-in; inspect the rule for delete/hide/external-forward actions. 2) Contain: if malicious, remove the rule, revoke sessions/tokens, reset credentials, and block any external forwarding target. 3) Hunt: review the mailbox for sent phishing/BEC, enumerate other mailboxes with rules created from the same IP, and check SharePoint/OneDrive for staged malicious documents.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules","Update-InboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("DeleteMessage","MarkAsRead","Deleted Items","Junk Email","RSS Feeds","RSS Subscriptions","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode, ActionType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| where Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage","MarkAsRead","Deleted Items","Junk Email","RSS Feeds","RSS Subscriptions","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Parameters, OfficeWorkload, OriginatingServer
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("New-InboxRule" OR "Set-InboxRule" OR "UpdateInboxRules")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication AADSignInEventsBeta
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode in (50074, 50076, 50158, 50125, 50097)
| extend MfaPrompt = AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
| where MfaPrompt
| summarize attempts = count(), distinct_ips = dcount(IPAddress)
    by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where attempts > 10
| order by attempts desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType == 50158        // MFA Challenge required / failed
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen  = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs       = make_set(IPAddress, 5)
            by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Attempts > 3               // tune to baseline
| order by Attempts desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication

    by _time span=5m, Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where count > 10
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication

    by _time span=5m, Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`

DeviceFileEvents

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

Critical TeamCity Flaw Could Let Attackers Run OS Commands Without Logging In

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 9 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

JetBrains is urging customers of on-premise versions of TeamCity to update to the latest version following the discovery of a critical security issue that could result in arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability, assigned CVE-2026-63077 (CVSS score: 9.8), affects all TeamCity On-Premises versions. It has been addressed in versions 2025.11.7 and 2026.1.3. TeamCity Cloud instances have already

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable TeamCity On-Premises exposed to CVE-2026-63077 (unauth agent-polling RCE) · [LLM] TeamCity server (java) process spawning an OS command interpreter — CVE-2026-63077 RCE · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Payload or JSP web shell written by the TeamCity server process — CVE-2026-63077
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 / reverse shell from TeamCity server process — CVE-2026-63077
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Vulnerable TeamCity On-Premises exposed to CVE-2026-63077 (unauth agent-polling RCE) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running TeamCity On-Premises builds still affected by CVE-2026-63077 (unauthenticated deserialization RCE in the agent polling protocol), prioritising internet-facing servers. This is the exposure hunt that scopes the blast radius before/while patching to 2025.11.7 or 2026.1.3. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and JetBrains' exact fixed builds (2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3) from the article; the internet-facing join operationalises JetBrains' own advice that even exposing the login screen/REST API is an entry point. Cross-checked JetBrains advisory, Help Net Security, and IONIX. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/28/teamcity-rce-cve-2026-63077-fixed/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.All_Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM catalog lag: a brand-new CVE may take 24-48h to map, yielding zero rows until Defender ingests it
  • TeamCity Cloud agents mislabelled as On-Premises in inventory (Cloud is not affected)
  • Servers already patched to 2025.11.7/2026.1.3 but TVM snapshot not yet refreshed
  • Dev/test TeamCity instances flagged as internet-facing behind a lab reverse proxy
  • Third-party CI images bundling an old TeamCity JRE that is not actually the running server
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SoftwareVersion is below 2025.11.7 (2025.x branch) or 2026.1.3 (2026.x branch) and check IsInternetFacing / perimeter exposure of the agent-polling port. 2) Contain: restrict the TeamCity server behind VPN/allow-list, or apply JetBrains' security-patch plugin (2017.1+) if a full upgrade cannot be scheduled immediately. 3) Hunt: on every affected host run UC2-UC4 (server process spawning shells, payload/webshell drops, outbound C2) over the exposure window to rule out pre-patch compromise; rotate any stored VCS/deploy credentials on confirmed-exposed servers.
