TeamCity server (java) process spawning an OS command interpreter — CVE-2026-63077 RCE AIExploitation High
Detects the TeamCity On-Premises server process (bundled java/javaw whose path or command line references TeamCity) spawning cmd/PowerShell/shell/LOLBins. Post-exploitation of CVE-2026-63077 runs OS commands with the server process's privileges; unlike build agents, the server itself should almost never launch interactive interpreters, making this high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchors on the article's core primitive — 'execute arbitrary OS commands with the privileges of the TeamCity server process' — while the buildAgent exclusion removes the single biggest FP source (agents legitimately spawn shells to run build steps; the server does not). Cross-checked JetBrains advisory and IONIX (CWE-502 deserialization in the polling protocol). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Server-side Versioned Settings / VCS operations spawning git.exe or svn.exe (excluded here by only matching interpreters/LOLBins, not VCS binaries)
  • Administrator-authored maintenance or backup scripts invoked from the server host
  • TeamCity server auto-update or diagnostics tooling launching a brief cmd.exe
  • Monitoring agents (health checks) running whoami/hostname under the java service context
  • A co-located build agent whose install path also contains 'TeamCity' but not 'buildAgent' — verify it is the server, not an agent
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "git" and ChildCmd !has "svn" and ChildCmd !has "hg.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "versionedSettings"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent java command line and the child ChildCmd — a server legitimately never runs ad-hoc cmd/powershell; look for recon (whoami, systeminfo), download (certutil/bitsadmin/curl), or encoded PowerShell. 2) Contain: isolate the host, suspend the TeamCity service, and block the server's agent-polling port at the perimeter; preserve the java process memory/logs. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC3 (payload/webshell writes by the same java PID) and UC4 (outbound C2), review TeamCity access logs around the spawn time, and rotate all stored build secrets, deploy keys, and connected-service tokens.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "teamcity" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "TeamCity"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "buildAgent" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "buildAgent"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","whoami.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","bash","sh","dash","curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has "TeamCity"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "java.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "javaw.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !has "buildAgent"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\whoami.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Payload or JSP web shell written by the TeamCity server process — CVE-2026-63077 AIInstallation Medium
Detects the TeamCity On-Premises server process (java/javaw or its shell child, path referencing TeamCity, excluding build agents) creating executable or script files — especially .jsp web shells dropped into the server's Java web root. Unauthenticated RCE via CVE-2026-63077 lets an attacker stage payloads or persistence directly in the server context. Rationale: Because TeamCity is a Java web application, a .jsp file written by the server java process into its web root is a textbook post-RCE web shell — a high-fidelity pivot distinct from the process-spawn UC. Grounded in the article's 'modification of server state' impact and CWE-502 deserialization confirmed by IONIX/JetBrains. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate TeamCity plugin install/upgrade writing .jar/.war (and sometimes .jsp) into the server directory
  • Server auto-update unpacking new binaries/DLLs during a maintenance window
  • Administrator manually deploying a custom plugin or diagnostic script
  • Backup or export jobs writing .bat/.ps1 helper scripts under the TeamCity data directory
  • Antivirus/quarantine tooling relocating files inside the TeamCity path (FileRenamed noise)
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName endswith ".jar" or FileName endswith ".war") or FolderPath has "webapps"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the written file — a .jsp/.war under the server web root or a new .exe/.ps1 outside a scheduled upgrade window is highly suspicious; hash it and check reputation. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, suspend the TeamCity service, and snapshot the host; if a web shell is confirmed, treat the server as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing java PID to UC2 (shell spawns) and UC4 (outbound C2), review web-access logs for requests to the dropped .jsp path, and search other CI/CD hosts for the same file hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "TeamCity" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "teamcity")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "buildAgent" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "buildAgent"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".jsp" or FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".ps1" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".war" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".sh"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "teamcity"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "buildAgent"
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("jsp","exe","ps1","bat","dll","war","vbs","sh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Executable or JSP Web Shell Written by TeamCity Server Process (CVE-2026-63077)

description: TeamCity On-Premises server process writing a script/executable or a .jsp web shell, consistent with payload staging or persistence after CVE-2026-63077 unauthenticated RCE.

Outbound C2 / reverse shell from TeamCity server process — CVE-2026-63077 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects public outbound network connections initiated by the TeamCity On-Premises server process (java under a TeamCity path, excluding build agents) on uncommon ports, or by a shell/LOLBin child of that java process. Post-exploitation of the unauthenticated RCE commonly beacons out or opens an interactive reverse shell from the server context. Rationale: Splits the signal two ways so it stays high-fidelity: a shell/LOLBin child of the TeamCity java process reaching any public IP, or the server java itself connecting outbound on non-web/non-SSH ports (reverse-shell / beacon ports). Anchored to the server-process-privileges impact described in the article and the RCE nature confirmed by JetBrains/Help Net Security. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/28/teamcity-rce-cve-2026-63077-fixed/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TeamCity server checking JetBrains for updates or fetching plugins over HTTPS (excluded by dropping 443/80)
  • Server-side VCS polling to an external Git/SVN host on a non-standard port
  • Integrations (issue trackers, cloud agents, artifact repos) that the server contacts on custom ports
  • Outbound SMTP/notification connectors from the server on port 25/587
  • Monitoring/APM agents co-located under the TeamCity path beaconing to a SaaS collector
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl endswith "jetbrains.com" or RemoteUrl endswith "github.com" or RemoteUrl endswith "githubusercontent.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl reputation and check whether the destination is a known JetBrains/VCS/integration endpoint; a shell-child-of-java connection or a raw IP on a reverse-shell port (4444/1337/9001/etc.) is high-priority. 2) Contain: block the destination at the egress firewall, isolate the host, and suspend the TeamCity service. 3) Hunt: correlate the connecting PID back to UC2 (shell spawn) and UC3 (payload drop), capture any beacon interval, and pivot on the remote IP/domain across all CI/CD and perimeter logs to find other affected servers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| extend anomaly = case(
    InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","bash","sh","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nc.exe","ncat.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java"), "shell-child-of-java",
    (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "TeamCity" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "buildAgent") and RemotePort !in (443, 80, 22), "teamcity-server-uncommon-port",
    "")
| where isnotempty(anomaly)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, anomaly, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

Researcher Says AI Helped Develop Linux Traffic-Control Race Into Root Exploit

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 9 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

STAR Labs has published a Linux kernel exploit that turns an ordinary local user into root on the CentOS Stream 9 build it targeted. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-53264 (CVSS score: 7.8), is a use-after-free race in the kernel's network traffic-control subsystem.Researcher Lee Jia Jie said artificial intelligence (AI) helped him find the bug and speed up exploit development. Linux core_pattern overwritten to memfd/pipe handler (CVE-2026-53264 privesc payoff) AIInstallation High
Hunts modification of /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern by a non-standard process — the final privilege-escalation step in the STAR Labs CVE-2026-53264 traffic-control UAF exploit, which overwrites core_pattern so a crashed child runs a memfd-backed binary as the root core-dump handler. core_pattern is a global setting normally touched only by systemd/sysctl at boot, so any other writer is high-signal. Rationale: Anchored on the exact procfs path (/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern) the article states the ROP chain overwrites; core_pattern is global and normally only written by systemd/sysctl, so a non-standard writer is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked NVD CVE-2026-53264 and Aqua Tracee's core_pattern_modification signature. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53264 • https://aquasecurity.github.io/tracee/v0.20/docs/events/builtin/signatures/core_pattern_modification/ • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-RHEL6-KERNELDOC-17568795
ATT&CKT1068 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • systemd-sysctl applying kernel.core_pattern from /etc/sysctl.d at boot
  • Admin manually running 'sysctl -w kernel.core_pattern=...' to configure coredumpctl/abrt
  • apport (Ubuntu) or abrt (RHEL) install hooks setting their pipe handler
  • Container runtime / kdump initialization writing core_pattern
  • Ansible/Chef/Puppet hardening playbooks enforcing a core_pattern baseline
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemd-sysctl","sysctl","systemd","apport","abrt-install-ccpp-hook","kdump","tuned","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the current core_pattern value on the host and the InitiatingProcess/ContextImage that wrote it — a value beginning with '|' pointing to a memfd, /tmp, or a deleted binary (not /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-coredump or apport) is malicious. Check the writer's UID and whether it was launched from a user namespace. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, capture the running process table and any process whose executable path is memfd/(deleted), and reset core_pattern to the distro default. 3) HUNT: Look on the same host for new user+network namespace creation, tc clsact/flower activity, and a root process executed from memfd within seconds of a child crash (UC 'Linux root fileless execution from memfd').
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has "/proc/sys/kernel" and FileName == "core_pattern"
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemd-sysctl","sysctl","systemd","apport","abrt-install-ccpp-hook","kdump","tuned","cloud-init")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Facility in ("audit","authpriv","kern","user") or ProcessName in ("auditd","audispd")
| where SyslogMessage has "core_pattern"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("name=\"/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern\"","/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern")
| where SyslogMessage !has "systemd-sysctl"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Linux root process executed from memfd (CVE-2026-53264 core-dump payload) AIExploitation High
Hunts a process running as root (UID 0) whose executable image is an anonymous memfd file. The CVE-2026-53264 exploit places a copy of itself in a memfd and deliberately crashes a child so the kernel runs the memfd-backed binary as the root core-dump handler in the init namespace — a fileless root execution with no on-disk binary. Rationale: Directly models the article's stated payoff — 'places a copy of itself in a memfd ... run the memfd-backed binary as the root core-dump handler.' A root-owned process whose image path is memfd is not produced by any legitimate service, giving very high fidelity. Corroborated against NVD CVE-2026-53264. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53264 • https://cyberpress.org/ai-helps-discover-linux-kernel-zero-day/
ATT&CKT1620 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit software using memfd_create + fexecve for sandboxed/anti-tamper loaders (some AV, DRM, or JIT runtimes)
  • Container tooling (e.g. runc/gVisor) that fexecs a memfd-sealed helper as root
  • Security research / red-team tooling on the host running fileless loaders
  • Package managers building in-memory transient binaries during a root install
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("runc","containerd-shim","dockerd")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the process ran as UID 0 and its image is memfd/(deleted) with no backing inode; capture the memfd contents (/proc/<pid>/exe) and hash it, and check the parent — kernel/core-dump context is the exploit tell. 2) CONTAIN: Kill the process, isolate the host, and snapshot memory before reboot to preserve the memfd payload. 3) HUNT: Correlate with a core_pattern modification and a deliberately crashed child process in the minute prior, plus new user/network namespace creation by the same unprivileged UID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has "memfd:" or FolderPath startswith "/memfd" or FileName startswith "memfd:"
| where AccountName == "root" or ProcessTokenElevation == "TokenElevationTypeFull"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ProcessName in ("auditd","audispd") or Facility == "audit"
| where SyslogMessage has "EXECVE" or SyslogMessage has "exe="
| where SyslogMessage has "memfd:"
| where SyslogMessage has "uid=0" or SyslogMessage has "euid=0"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unprivileged Linux tc clsact/flower/gact traffic-control manipulation (CVE-2026-53264 trigger) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a non-root user driving the traffic-control path the CVE-2026-53264 UAF requires — a clsact qdisc plus a flower classifier and gact action (CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER / CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT). Surfaces the exploit's setup stage where an unprivileged process gains namespace-local CAP_NET_ADMIN and races RTM_NEWTFILTER/RTM_DELTFILTER. Hunting tier: a compiled exploit uses raw netlink and will not spawn the tc binary, but interactive tc use of clsact+flower by a normal user is itself anomalous. Rationale: Uses the exact kernel feature names the article and NVD cite (clsact qdisc, CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER 'flower' classifier, CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT 'gact' action) on the tc binary by a non-root user. Marked hunting because the PoC uses raw netlink (no tc process) — this catches interactive/adapted variants, not the compiled exploit. Corroborated by NVD/Snyk on the tcf_idr_check_alloc UAF path. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53264 • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-RHEL6-KERNELDOC-17568795
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kubernetes CNI plugins (Cilium, Calico) programming clsact/flower TC filters — often run as root though
  • Network engineers testing QoS/traffic shaping with tc in a lab
  • eBPF/XDP tooling that attaches clsact qdiscs
  • Container network setup scripts invoking tc during pod bring-up
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cilium-agent","calico-node","kubelet","containerd")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the invoking UID is unprivileged and whether the tc call occurred inside a freshly created user/network namespace (check /proc/<pid>/ns); legitimate TC programming is usually root or a CNI service account. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, isolate the host and snapshot the process tree — the qdisc setup is the pre-race stage, so root compromise may be seconds away. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host/UID for core_pattern modification and a root memfd execution; check kernel version against the CVE-2026-53264 fixed releases.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("clsact","flower","gact")
| where AccountName !in~ ("root","system") and AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog

| where ProcessName in ("auditd","audispd") or Facility == "audit"
| where SyslogMessage has "EXECVE"
| where SyslogMessage has "/tc" and (SyslogMessage has "clsact" or SyslogMessage has "flower" or SyslogMessage has "gact")
| where SyslogMessage !has "uid=0"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CVE-2026-53264 unpatched kernel exposure (traffic-control UAF LPE) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces onboarded Linux hosts still carrying a kernel vulnerable to CVE-2026-53264. With full exploit source public and per-kernel ROP offsets, exposure prioritisation matters: fixed releases are 5.10.259, 5.15.210, 6.1.176, 6.6.143, 6.12.94, 6.18.36, 7.0.13. Pairs with the behavioural UCs to distinguish 'exposed' from 'exploited'. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE id and the exact fixed kernel releases the article enumerates; a straight TVM/vuln-DM lookup on CVE-2026-53264 gives a clean, no-FP exposure list. Cross-checked NVD and Snyk records for the same CVE id. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53264 • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-RHEL6-KERNELDOC-17568795
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scanner reports the CVE on a kernel already patched via distro backport but with an unchanged upstream version string (Debian/Ubuntu backports) — verify the distro package build, not the mainline number
  • Hosts lacking unprivileged user namespaces or CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT/CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER are exposed-but-not-exploitable
  • Stale TVM inventory after a kernel update but before reboot
  • Duplicate device entries inflating the exposed count
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each flagged host confirm the running kernel vs the distro-fixed build (not upstream number), and check whether unprivileged user namespaces and the CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT/CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER options are enabled — that narrows truly exploitable hosts. 2) CONTAIN: For exploitable hosts, apply the distro kernel update and reboot; as interim mitigation set kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 where the workload allows. 3) HUNT: On any exposed host, run the core_pattern-modification and memfd-root-execution UCs to check for prior exploitation attempts.

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-53264")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-53264")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

NightLedger DLL side-load: SspiCli.dll loaded by AppVShNotify.exe from non-System32 path AIInstallation High
Hunts Mirage Kitten's NightLedger backdoor which masquerades as SspiCli.dll and is loaded via search-order hijacking against a co-located legitimate AppVShNotify.exe (which delay-loads SspiCli.dll through RPCRT4.dll). Legitimate SspiCli.dll only ever loads from System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS, so a load from any other directory (or the known sample MD5) is high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact sideload chain (SspiCli.dll masquerade + AppVShNotify.exe + non-System32 origin) plus the confirmed sample MD5 c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac; legit SspiCli.dll only loads from Windows system dirs so the path predicate is inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nimbus-manticore-deploys-nightledger.html • https://www.technadu.com/mirage-kittens-new-malware-toolkit-targets-aerospace-and-defense-across-middle-east-and-africa/632036/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001/
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate App-V AppVShNotify.exe running from its default Client directory (excluded by path filter)
  • Security tooling copying appvshnotify.exe into a sandbox/quarantine folder for analysis
  • Software packaging/repackaging tools staging App-V binaries in a build directory
  • Developer machines with App-V SDK test harnesses placing the binary in a project folder
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Application Virtualization") and not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Application Virtualization")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the loaded-DLL folder path and SHA256/MD5 for SspiCli.dll; confirm AppVShNotify.exe is running outside the App-V Client dir and check code-signing/prevalence of both files. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the AppVShNotify.exe process tree, and quarantine the co-located SspiCli.dll; capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: sweep the estate for the same MD5 and for AppVShNotify.exe outside its install path, then pivot to network egress toward realhealthshop.com/tjconsultingservices.com and the NightLedger URI endpoints to confirm C2.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "sspicli.dll" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "appvshnotify.exe"
         and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32")
         and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64")
         and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"))
     or MD5 == "c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll=FileName, LoadedDllPath=FolderPath, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\appvshnotify.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Application Virtualization\Client")
     and not(NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Application Virtualization\Client")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NightLedger C2 beacon to Mirage Kitten domains and distinctive URI endpoints AICommand & Control High
Hunts NightLedger command-and-control: HTTPS beacons to realhealthshop[.]com (primary) and tjconsultingservices[.]com (fallback), plus the two other campaign domains, and the highly distinctive random-looking URI paths used for tasking (/edfcvfgbhnjmkqwasderfgg), file upload (/qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj) and command output (/wsdefvvbnhyuijkplmbgfrtt) visible in TLS-inspecting proxy logs. Rationale: Uses the exact NightLedger C2 domains and the three verbatim tasking/upload/output URI endpoints from the article; the domains are corroborated by The Hacker News and TechNadu, and the URIs are effectively unique so any proxy-visible hit is a strong true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nimbus-manticore-deploys-nightledger.html • https://blog.polyswarm.io/mirage-kitten-deploys-nightledger-backdoor-in-espionage-campaign-targeting-the-middle-east-and-africa
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS sinkhole services probing the domains
  • Web content filters pre-fetching URLs for categorization
  • Analyst manually browsing to the IOC domain during triage
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect AppVShNotify.exe / rundll32-style host) and confirm the destination is one of the four IOC domains or a distinctive URI; check whether the source host also shows the SspiCli.dll sideload. 2) Contain: block the four domains and any resolved IPs at proxy/firewall, isolate the beaconing host. 3) Hunt: search the same host for POST traffic to /qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj and /wsdefvvbnhyuijkplmbgfrtt (exfil/output), enumerate other hosts resolving these domains, and pivot to BridgeHead WebSocket egress to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("realhealthshop.com","tjconsultingservices.com","businessmixture.com","aecert.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

     or RequestURL has_any ("/edfcvfgbhnjmkqwasderfgg","/qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj","/wsdefvvbnhyuijkplmbgfrtt")

BridgeHead/ArcBridge WebSocket tunneler dropped at hardcoded Mirage Kitten paths AIInstallation High
Hunts the drop of Mirage Kitten's WebSocket SOCKS5 tunnelers, deployed as unbcl.dll under %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\VisualStudio and as libwinpthread-1.dll under \univpn\promote. Both are otherwise-legitimate DLL names, so anchoring on the specific abnormal directories yields a high-fidelity file-drop signal. Rationale: Anchored on the two verbatim deployment paths from the article (%LocalAppData%\Microsoft\VisualStudio\unbcl.dll and C:\program files (x86)\univpn\promote\libwinpthread-1.dll); pairing the common DLL names with those abnormal directories keeps FPs near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nimbus-manticore-deploys-nightledger.html • https://www.techtimes.com/articles/321943/20260729/iran-deploys-nightledger-backdoor-websocket-relays-across-six-nations.htm
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine MinGW-built application legitimately shipping libwinpthread-1.dll (but under its own install dir, not \univpn\promote)
  • Visual Studio component caches placing MFC runtime DLLs — unbcl.dll normally lives in System32/SysWOW64, not the VisualStudio LocalAppData tree
  • Software installer extracting a redistributable into an unusual staging folder
  • Backup/restore tooling rehydrating user AppData
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped DLL and record the writing process; confirm the path matches the abnormal VisualStudio/univpn locations and that the file is unsigned/low-prevalence. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the DLL, and terminate any process that has it mapped (check for rundll32 or a renamed host loading it). 3) Hunt: look for the outbound WebSocket to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net from this host, the GetUserNameA username-gate behavior, and repeat the file sweep across aerospace/telecom endpoints for the same two path patterns.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "unbcl.dll" and FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\VisualStudio")
     or (FileName =~ "libwinpthread-1.dll" and FolderPath has @"\univpn\promote")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "unbcl.dll" and TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\VisualStudio")
     or (TargetFileName =~ "libwinpthread-1.dll" and TargetFilePath has @"\univpn\promote")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BridgeHead WebSocket SOCKS5 tunnel to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net AICommand & Control High
Hunts BridgeHead's covert channel: an HTTPS WebSocket (GET /connect, Upgrade: websocket) to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net that, after a 'token' auth frame, becomes a full SOCKS5 relay. Detection anchors on the specific Azure App Service C2 host and the hardcoded legacy Edge 86 User-Agent string in proxy telemetry. Rationale: Uses the exact BridgeHead C2 FQDN (smartconnect.azurewebsites.net) and the hardcoded legacy Edge 86 User-Agent from the article; the SOCKS5-over-WebSocket relay design and Azure App Service abuse match Check Point's Nimbus Manticore Azure-C2 reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/nimbus-manticore-deploys-new-malware-targeting-europe/ • https://www.technadu.com/mirage-kittens-new-malware-toolkit-targets-aerospace-and-defense-across-middle-east-and-africa/632036/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572/
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal app genuinely hosted on the same Azure App Service host name (verify tenant ownership)
  • Legacy browsers/agents still emitting Chrome/Edge 86 User-Agents on unrelated traffic
  • Security scanners or uptime monitors probing azurewebsites.net endpoints
  • Developer testing WebSocket services against an *.azurewebsites.net staging slot
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is not a browser (BridgeHead runs from a sideloaded DLL host); check for a persistent bidirectional/WebSocket-upgraded session and the Edg/86.0.622.38 UA. 2) Contain: block smartconnect.azurewebsites.net and resolved IPs, isolate the host, and terminate the tunneling process. 3) Hunt: correlate with the unbcl.dll/libwinpthread-1.dll drop and NightLedger C2 on the same host, review internal SOCKS-relayed destinations reached through the victim (lateral targets), and sweep for other hosts resolving the same Azure host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where HttpHostName has "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net" or Url has "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net"
| extend SuspiciousUA = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has "Edg/86.0.622.38"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, SuspiciousUA
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or SHA1 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or MD5 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or SHA1 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or MD5 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
